articles.title: A look into the SGA Advisor position
articles.description: The Student Government Association (SGA) is the University's representative body for undergraduate students. Members of the SGA can either be elected directly by the student body or appointed by members of the organization. As the official representative and policy-making body, the SGA and its members not only aim to advocate for the rights of students, but also to improve their experience at the University. "The Student Government Association (SGA) at Johns Hopkins University is the primary representative body of undergraduate students. It is a student-run organization that is responsible for representing the interests of the student body to the University's administration," the homepage of the SGA website reads. The SGA is a Registered Student Organization (RSO), like many official clubs or organizations on campus. The Office of Leadership Engagement & Experiential Development (LEED) oversees RSOs in matters of registration, event planning and general oversight. As an RSO, the SGA is expected to follow the expectations for organizations that LEED puts out. One of such requirements is that all RSOs must have an advisor who is a faculty or staff member of the University. "Registered Student Organizations are required to have a faculty/staff advisor at the school where the organization is affiliated that is in good standing with the university," LEED's website states. LEED additionally states that faculty advisors must abide by University policies, and make sure that the organizations they oversee do so as well. "The prospective advisor must acknowledge and commit to upholding university policies. The university or school reserves the right to approve, remove, or reassign an advisor to a student organization at its discretion, including but not limited to circumstances in which the faculty member is no longer in good standing or is otherwise unable to fulfill the advisor requirements," LEED outlines in its advisor requirements. As an RSO, SGA has multiple assigned faculty advisors. LEED, however, does not state how involved advisors have to be in their organizations, nor what their required responsibilities are besides upholding University rules. The SGA's Constitution, which was recently amended on Sept. 18, does not explicitly define a role for its advisor. In fact, the word "advisor" is not used in the Constitution. The Bylaws of the SGA, which were also amended on the same date as the Constitution, establish the existence of an advisor in the document's seventh article, but do not necessarily indicate specific functions of the role. "There shall exist SGA advisors who shall be resources when called upon by the SGA," one section of the bylaws states. In addition to establishing the role's existence, the bylaws also specify how many advisors the organization needs. "The SGA, in conjunction with the Office of the Dean of Student Life may appoint one (1) SGA Advisor for the SGA at large, one (1) Class Council Advisor for each council, one (1) Finance advisor for the Committee on Finance, and one (1) Student Organizations Advisor for the Committee on Student Organizations," the bylaws includes. The seventh article in a previous edition of the bylaws, written in April 2026, features identical text, indicating that the section had been left unchanged when the SGA was drafting new bylaws. The Committee on Student Elections is the student-run organization closely linked with the SGA that oversees elections. Their constitution, like the SGA's, also does not make any mention of advisors. While the existence and amount of advisors for the organization are made explicit, the bylaws do not define a specific function for the advisors to perform, other than acting as a resource, a term which is not defined in the bylaws. According to the University, in an email to The News-Letter, the advisor's role is to make sure University policies are being enforced, while at the same time supporting the SGA members in their policy making and outreach work. "The SGA advisor is a university staff member whose responsibilities include supporting and advising the SGA. The advisor serves in that capacity as part of their university role and provides guidance on university policies, procedures, and resources while supporting the work of SGA's elected student leaders," the University spokesperson wrote. In addition, multiple members of SGA have discussed their experiences with the role of the SGA advisor in interviews with The News-Letter. One current senator, who wished to remain anonymous under the pseudonym Aiden, expressed their frustration with SGA advisor role. "When I reach out to departments for meetings or with questions, instead of being able to talk to someone and express student concerns, someone in the department will loop in an advisor and drag out the process for several weeks or even months to schedule a meeting with all parties," Aiden wrote in an email interview with The News-Letter. Specifically, Aiden shared that they believe the advisor role can make communication between members of the SGA and administration more difficult, and that this function of the advisor role may be intentional. "I see the advisor role as a way for administration and departments to avoid transparency and open dialogue with actual students. This is by no means a critique of individual advisors, but rather the role as a whole and the way it is used as a buffer between students and the people they need answers from," Aiden wrote. Another member of SGA, choosing to comment anonymously under the pseudonym Robin, shared generally positive experiences working with SGA advisors, in which they said that advisors would make efforts to connect with senators and support them with any questions they had. "They get to know each [SGA member] very well and will make personal connections with each one and offer answers to any questions," Robin shared. Robin also referenced an informal policy where SGA representatives are reminded to cc SGA advisors into emails sent from the members to University administration to ensure visibility, emphasizing that it was not for authorization nor were any member prevented from contacting anyone. The News-Letter was unable to find any information on this in their guiding documents. Robin clarified that advisors cannot enforce rules on communication for SGA. One SGA member from the 2020-21 Executive Board, choosing to comment under the pseudonym Parker, shared their experience working with the advisors, noting that there were no communication enforcements under their term as well in an email to The News-Letter. "When I was involved in SGA, advisors offeredto assist in facilitating discussion with University administration if we requested. If we liked, they could make the initial outreach for us when reaching out to a specific member of the University administration and cc us on the email chain. They requested that we cc them on all email communications with members of the University Administration, which we usually complied with to help facilitate a good working relationship but were not required to do," Parker wrote. During the 2020-2021 term, Parker recalled how the advisors held regular meetings with the Executive Board, which at the time were required by the SGA Constitution, and spoke at GBMs. Another current SGA representative, choosing to comment under the pseudonym Blake, commented that SGA advisors tend to communicate with administration about SGA-related matters without keeping members informed, which limits avenues for accountability. "SGA advisors claim they act for the benefit of students and fight on SGA's behalf when they communicate with University Administration. In reality, SGA advisors generally take SGA's communications up the chain and will avoid copying or including SGA members in further communications, so there is no way SGA can evaluate if this is the case," Robin said. Since the SGA has been an official organization ever since it was established in its current form in 2008, after its renaming from Student Council, the SGA has had an advisor since its founding. Evan Lazerowitz, who graduated from the University in 2010, provided comment about his experience with his SGA advisor, which he described as somewhat less involved than the experiences of contemporary SGA members. "In my tenure on student government, our advisor, was very hands off and advised us from behind the scenes, letting students make informed decisions that were free from interference from the SGA advisor," Lazerowitz wrote in an email interview to The News-Letter. Jazzlyn Fernandez, a senior who currently serves as President of the Senate in SGA, also gave comment on her relationship with advisors, which she framed as helpful, especially in the advisors' ability to connect students with administration and other departments within the University. "As President of the Senate now, I have found the role of the SGA advisor to take on a new form. We ('we' being the advisor and I) meet weekly to talk about different goals that I have for the Senate, as well as how to best serve the Senators so that they can work on their own initiatives. This meeting is a space where we feel free to have different opinions, and come to understand the different views that we have to best serve the Senate, as well as the Johns Hopkins undergraduate student body. The SGA advisor gives guidance to any Senator or Executive member who requests it, including myself, and provides connections to different administrative bodies so that we may be able to collaborate for the benefit of all students," Fernandez wrote. Honora Muratori is a News & Features Editor for The News-Letter and Executive Secretary for SGA. She was not involved in the reporting or writing of this article. Katherine Zhu is a News & Features Editor for The News-Letter and a Student Justice in the Judiciary Board for SGA. She was not involved in the reporting or writing of this article.

articles.title: What SGA owes University administration
articles.description: In April 2026, The News-Letter reached out to members of the Student Government Association's (SGA) Executive Board to encourage SGA members to write about their progress regarding recent initiatives, the reason behind pursuing them and potential concerns about SGA's trajectory. Our reason for this was simple: We wish to expand our coverage to all aspects of student life, which SGA plays a large role in. Although The News-Letter covers the weekly SGA general body meetings (GBM), these are brief 400-500 word articles that lack insight that SGA representatives could provide if they wrote their own articles. In addition, while SGA collectively posts updates on Instagram, the information shared is restricted by thesocial media format. We believed that The News-Letter would serve as a platform for SGA to archive their legislative progress and increase their transparency for the student body, a goal SGA has been making headway on in recent years. SGA invited The News-Letter to call for SGA columnists at their first public GBM on Sept. 1, 2026. During the meeting, The News-Letter emphasized that all articles written by SGA members would feature a disclaimer stating that the opinion expressed solely belongs to the writer, not the entirety of SGA. Following The News-Letter's departure, an SGA staff advisor urged members to consult the Executive Board and an SGA advisor prior to writing for The News-Letter. Multiple SGA members alerted The News-Letter regarding this announcement, citing how the advisor cautioned them about criticizing SGA and University administration. This alarmed us. The News-Letter is founded upon a commitment to student's free speech, and the possibility for conflicting dialogue to be filtered may prevent the dialogue from occurring altogether. Is the role of administration in SGA to advise the personal expression of every student who also serves as an SGA representative? On Sept. 10, an SGA member emailed Vice Provost for Student Affairs Rachelle Hernandez, asking for clarification on the administration's stance on SGA expression, especially for public criticism. The next day, The News-Letter requested a formal directive from the SGA Executive Board, which would explicate its policy regarding SGA members' participation with The News-Letter. We did not suggest anything specific to be included in that directive -we simply asked for it to be delivered. Shortly after these requests, the advisor's initial statement was later redacted by another SGA advisor at the Sept. 15 GBM. The advisor stated that SGA members do not require approval from administration to write for The News-Letter. We noted that "consultation," as stated by the other SGA advisor, and approval are not synonymous. The advisor also encouraged SGA to construct their own policies regarding contributing. We worried how the two contradictory announcements would affect SGA member enthusiasm for contributing to The News-Letter. On Sept. 29, SGA passed the "JHU SGA Freedom Of Expression Directive," which reiterates and defends the public speech of SGA members. Notable sections regarding administrative input include establishing the lack of a mandatory review by administrative members, encouraging "agreement, disagreement, critique, and commentary on SGA actions, administrative actions, and campus issues." The Directive also offers SGA members the choice of optional feedback from administration. After the first GBM and prior to the passing of the Directive, we examined SGA's guiding documents, such as the Constitution and Bylaws of the Senate, to analyze the authority and responsibilities SGA advisors and administration hold. On the one hand, the Constitution does not mention the scope of the SGA advisor. On the other hand, the Bylaws of the Senate defined the advisors as "resources when called upon by the SGA." Scattered responsibilities included meeting with SGA members to "develop a strategy for increasing student interest and engagement," dealing with accommodation requests for SGA events and other tasks. There was no mention of overseeing SGA member speech. While reflecting on the role of the University administration in monitoring student organizations, we realized that the reverse also merited contemplation. To borrow the syntax shared by the University President Ronald J. Daniels in the title of his co-authored book What Universities Owe Democracy, what do student organizations, particularly ones central to student expression such as SGA, owe to the University administration? In the first pages of his book, Daniels affirms all institutions' aversion to change, especially in moments of uncertainty. "This is especially the case for colleges and universities," Daniels writes. However, Daniels also notes that "within such institutions, meaningful transformation becomes truly possible only during periods of change and profound uncertainty. Economists call these 'critical junctures.'" It seems the University itself would appear to be at such a "critical juncture." We recognize that higher education is currently facing scrutiny from the federal government, particularly in securing federal funding and navigating new higher education frameworks. Regarding the mention of "meaningful transformation," we believe that student organizations, especially SGA, have the potential to advocate for institutional changes to administration. We are strongly aware of SGA's importance on campus; they are the only organization that can directly connect University administration with student concerns, compromise on fair, lasting changes through legislation and establish the groundwork for administration's external oversight. This is precisely what SGA owes to University administration. For SGA to continue bridging students to administration, it must still listen and communicate to students on its own accord, uninfluenced by any administrative pressure in the process. Moreover, if student representatives or entire organizations themselves become prone to routine self-censorship, who's to say that this habit, rooted in fear, will not spread to the greater student body and become engrained in student culture? We support SGA's commitment to maintaining free speech internally, but we are aware that, even in this newly passed Directive, the role of administration in SGA expression is solely defined by what they cannot do, rather than what they can. The role of Hopkins administration in SGA should be clearly defined in its guiding documents and be adhered to so that student leaders, and the student body as a whole, can distinguish between fair administrative guidance and restriction on student voices. Now, SGA must continue meticulously outlining and protecting their free expression, and University administration should uphold its expressed commitment to let SGA internally decide how to manage its oversight for external publication. To SGA members: The News-Letter will continue to report on and preserve your progress. Now, we hope you feel welcome to do the same. The Editorial Board consists of the Editors-in-Chief, the Managing Editors, the Opinions Editor, and one Editor-at-Large from any section other than News & Features. The Editorial Board operates independently from the reporting conducted by the News & Features section.

articles.title: You don't have to do it all
articles.description: Before I came to Hopkins, my world was one of gilded excess. Flaky silver high school signs, faded yellow restaurants always boasting about having the "most," old cars with big logos and peeling paint. Coming from a low-income, majority immigrant area meant I was always surrounded by excess. There was an obsession with collection and preservation - take, for example, how I've never seen the back wall of my grandma's garage, despite working away at the pile for 10 summers. I worry that new Hopkins students overfill their garages, too, overly preoccupied with the idea of "never enough." I would never blame the freshmen (a year of experience does not amount to much in wisdom). They are promised fanciful positions and opportunities. And for how hard they work, rightfully so! But being overwhelmed with jobs, extracurriculars, internships, research, any pursuit they could dream of, anything new they could try - I think that is a great advantage for those who had more growing up, compared to those who have less. It is advantageous to grow up having more options, to be able to choose. I say this specifically for people who come from environments like mine: the definition of success was joining everything that my under-resourced high school allowed me to do. We did not ask each other about what organizations we thought were important, only the number. We grew up hoarding belongings; it only made sense to hoard our opportunities, too. I've seen too many students step into the waters of Hopkins and immediately start to drown. Not because they're overwhelmed, but because they choose to be overwhelmed. Perhaps they do not know how to choose, how to commit or how to quit the haphazard things they somewhat love. And in exchange, they lose the depth in what they love the most, what is actually most important to them. This is not meant to discourage anyone, at any point, from trying new things. I've grown the most through my discovered love for a cappella, something that I would've never dreamt of joining during high school. But there is a difference between having a taste and deciding to swallow the plate. Something that surprised me about Hopkins was the depth of the organizations and commitments that someone could join. It was quite easy to "accidentally" fall into an officer position for the year, into multiple six to eight hour commitments during the first month of school. For those who grew up with choice, it might be easier to distinguish one's wants and needs, what someone could realistically commit to and accomplish. But I argue that for those who see every opportunity at Hopkins as a diamond of equal size, the choice is either too paralyzing or too heavy to cash into the bank. There is no doubt that every student at Hopkins could do absolutely amazing, incredible things. I think the problem will always be the time. Not that we don't have enough, but many of us would choose to fill every overlapping gap in that schedule - the time during which we are meant to live. Between all of the responsibilities and the preparations for jobs and graduate school, there has to be time to start anew. To be true to ourselves. It took me the entirety of freshman year to realize that I don't have to have it all. I don't have to do it all. Sticking with a few clubs, with a few meaningful things, might just be enough. And it helps the gold shine - the one under the leaf and the plaster, the stickers and the scraps. I remember the last conversation I had before I flew to Hopkins this year was in Joshua Tree, sending off one of my friends to their first year in college. And the greatest message was this: "The hardest, most impressive thing someone can do isn't necessarily what's meant for them." So slow down. Decide what you want to do, explore different options, create a path of your own. You don't have to see it all now. Take it easy, Blue Jays. You'll accomplish everything you want to and more, I promise. Andrew Huynh is a sophomore from Garden Grove, Calif. majoring in Neuroscience. His column, "Ad Astra," captures his reflections on modern life and Hopkins as he navigates his transition into adulthood.

articles.title: Hopkins students rethink who gets to do protein engineering
articles.description: As complicated as it may sound, protein engineering can seem like a field reserved for professionals with years of specialized training. One undergraduate team at Hopkins, however, is challenging that assumption. UPET, a student-led protein engineering group at Hopkins, has been selected as one of 30 teams worldwide for the top track of an international protein design competition supported by Anthropic and Adaptyv Bio. The so-called "Track 1" is meant "for labs and companies with significant protein design expertise and experts in at least one competition problem area." As a result, UPET received $50,000 in Claude credits, $10,000 in GPU computing resources from Modal and guaranteed experimental testing for dozens of its protein designs. The group is mentored by Jeffrey Gray, a professor of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering at the Whiting School of Engineering and principal investigator of the Gray Lab, which researches computational and structural prediction and design involving glycans, membrane proteins and protein crystals. The protein engineering UPET works on spans a wide range of complex problems. At its most basic level, however, protein engineering involves designing or modifying proteins to perform a desired function. This could mean altering an existing enzyme so it breaks down materials - such as plastic - more efficiently, developing a protein drug that binds to a viral target or creating an entirely new protein with properties that have not previously existed in nature. In the Anthropic competition, UPET is tasked with designing, among others, intelligent therapeutics for next-generation medicine, including a pH-sensing tumor-specific EGFR binder for the first week. In an interview with The News-Letter, Jonathan Ouyang, founder and president of UPET, explained the versality of protein engineering, both as a field that allows researchers to both modify existing proteins and design entirely new ones. "You can either take existing proteins and adapt them, or, increasingly, you can generate proteins de novo, or from scratch," Ouyang explained. Ouyang had been drawn to protein engineering even before coming to Hopkins because of its potential to improve human health and quality of life. "When I was going to college, I just wanted to do protein engineering," Ouyang said. That drive eventually became UPET: a space for undergraduates to simply do protein engineering.UPET is unique in its structure. It differs from a traditional research lab in one important way: students do not need years of prior experience before they can begin contributing. The structure also creates a fast-paced learning environment that differs from traditional academic work. Yash Bhargava, UPET's simulation expert, described the pace of the competition in an email interview with The News-Letter. "One thing I enjoy about UPET is how fast-paced it is. Right now, we're participating in a competition where a new challenge is released every week, requiring a very different approach from traditional academic work. We're pushed to understand a new biological problem, come up with design approaches, test different methods and iterate almost immediately," Bhargava said. More than half of the organization's members have no previous background in protein design and come from a variety of disciplines, ranging from Cognitive Science to Biophysics. Rather than treating that as a barrier, UPET has made education one of its central priorities. With an emphasis on democratizing access to protein engineering, Ouyang believes the field is far more accessible than many students assume. "These are things that are much more accessible than the average person thinks they are," Ouyang said. Ouyang compared scientific research with activities such as writing or playing music. Students often feel comfortable practicing those activities without asking for permission, he explained, while research can feel as though it requires passing through several institutional gates first. "You can do real, good work," Ouyang said, "and you don't have to be screened by a lab or be mentored for years." But Ouyang's ambitions for UPET extend beyond making protein engineering more accessible. He also sees AI fundamentally changing what undergraduate researchers can design. With support from Anthropic, Ouyang hopes to expand the role of AI in protein design beyond prediction models and models trained on raw data. He envisions using agentic AI systems to oversee multiple aspects of the design process, including reasoning over biological data, interpreting experimental results and proposing how a molecule should be changed next. Traditionally, scientists examine a structure and decide whether to alter a charged region, introduce a new interaction or mutate particular amino acids. AI systems may increasingly be able to participate in that reasoning process, making protein engineering more efficient. For Ouyang, the competition is only the beginning. He envisions UPET growing into a hub for original research, patented protein designs and collaborations with Hopkins laboratories to design proteins, and, eventually, into a group capable of hosting a protein design competition of its own.

articles.title: New protein-based membranes aim to separate lithium from sodium for battery production
articles.description: UK researchers aim to use engineered protein membranes with tiny pores to separate lithium from sodium for battery production.

From personal experience, many of us can attest that people who smoke weed are usually the chillest folks in the room. articles.title: Sentinel-3C returns its first views of Earth
articles.description: Just two weeks after it was launched, the Copernicus Sentinel-3C satellite returned its first images and measurements from two of its key instruments—a major milestone that confirms the satellite is working well and on track to monitor the health of Earth's oceans, land, cryosphere and atmosphere.

articles.title: Informal food vendors: The invisible backbone of the world's food system
articles.description: Walk through almost any city or town in a low-income or middle-income country and you'll pass them: the woman selling deep-fried fish from a cart, the mobile vendor with a bicycle full of vegetables, the kiosk operator who's the only source of a hot meal within walking distance. Food systems employ an estimated 1.23 billion people globally, and a majority of those jobs are informal—unlicensed, unregistered or otherwise outside the reach of formal regulation. In low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs) especially, informal vendors are not a marginal feature of how people eat; they are a linchpin of food security and livelihoods for over a billion people.

articles.title: Fossil bite marks suggest first evidence of a small raptor feeding on an apex predator
articles.description: A prehistoric cold case near Drumheller reveals either a small-time raptor scavenged on an apex predator, or a baby Albertosaurus engaged in a shocking act of cannibalism. These two possible explanations for what happened to an Albertosaurus after its death near Drumheller are wildly divergent.

articles.title: New framework links digital technology and mineral processing to support Africa's economic growth
articles.description: Research published in the International Journal of Business Innovation and Research (IJBIR) suggests that African economies need to move beyond fragmented development strategies. This might be done by uniting digital technology, startup networks, resource processing and cross-sector partnerships into a single societal innovation ecosystem, the researchers explain.

articles.title: Mars' Odd 1,100 Mile Long Cloud Forms in Mysterious Ways — a New Model May Reveal How
articles.description: Learn more about the AMEC, a strange, recurring cloud on Mars that has long baffled scientists, until now.

articles.title: New 'computational microscope' simulates DNA packaging at more than ten times previous scale
articles.description: The DNA in our cells wraps around proteins called histones to form nucleosomes, which organize into chromatin. This organization helps pack genetic material into the nucleus and influences how easily genes can be read and DNA damage repaired. Understanding how chromatin changes requires studying molecular movements and interactions that are difficult to capture experimentally.

articles.title: Chemists uncover the true active surface of nickel catalysts
articles.description: Nickel is a promising, cost-effective and robust catalyst for alkaline water electrolysis—a key technology for the climate-neutral production of hydrogen. However, the actual structure of the active surface of such nickel electrodes under reaction conditions had not yet been conclusively determined. A research team at Ulm University has now refuted a decades-old assumption: The catalytically active surface does not consist of nickel oxyhydroxide (NiOOH), as was previously widely assumed, but is nickel dioxide (NiO₂). The findings have been published in the journal Nature Catalysis.

articles.title: Bavaria's ancestral languages: Resisting linguistic genocide
articles.description: My ancestral languages, Boarisch (Bavarian) and Schwäbisch (Swabian), are routinely described as German dialects. That might sound like a technical linguistic distinction. For me, a Boarisch-Schwob scholar and community member, it raises a practical question: What happens to a people when their ancestral language, which carries their identity and "Weltanschauung" (worldview), is excluded from protection under a European language treaty because the modern state and dominant culture reduce it to a dialect?

articles.title: How to see the meteor shower that won’t keep you up all night | CNN
articles.description: See up to 10 meteors per hour during the Draconids, peaking Thursday night into Friday morning.

articles.title: Electronic stripes linked to unusual vortex states in a superconductor
articles.description: Superconductors, materials that can carry electric current with an electrical resistance of zero, have proved to be promising for the development of various technologies, including medical devices, particle accelerators and quantum computers. Studying these materials could help researchers uncover new physical states that could be useful for specific applications.

articles.title: This Disembodied Hand Is All the Robot You Need
articles.description: A hand attached to the end of an arm is a given for most humans, but what if robots didn’t have to play by the same rules as we do? Researchers from ETH Zurich have turned an off-the-shelf robotic hand into a completely self-contained robot that walks on its fingertips while using those same fingers to manipulate its environment. Besides making the perfect Halloween accessory for anyone planning to dress up as a member of The Addams Family – who were famously accompanied by a disembodied walking hand called Thing – the researchers say the approach could make it possible to operate controls and handle objects in places a traditional robot arm can’t reach. Amirhossein Kazemipour, a Ph.D. candidate in the Soft Robotics Lab at ETH Zurich in Switzerland who led the project, believes this hand could prove useful in contexts like fiddly maintenance tasks in industrial settings, or in search and rescue, where a robot could detach its hand to explore confined spaces too tight for the rest of its body. More broadly, he says, the work is a step toward a new approach to robotics in which body parts are not confined to a single role. “I wanted to see how much a robotic hand could do without the rest of the robot,” Kazemipour told IEEE Spectrum. “Instead of having this traditional view of robotic parts, what if we could use those parts to do other tasks that they are not designed to do.” This is not the first attempt to get a robot hand to walk, but previous work has typically relied on specially designed hands. The ETH team instead decided to use off-the-shelf hardware from Wuji Technology, augmented with an 80-gram backpack containing a battery, an inertial measurement unit (IMU), and a Raspberry Pi Zero. Kazemipour says they decided to go with a commercial robot hand because they didn’t want to compromise on the hand’s manipulation capabilities. This introduced significant challenges, he adds, because a hand’s shape is optimized for grasping rather than crawling. How to Walk With Fingers To teach the hand to walk, the researchers trained a model in simulation using reinforcement learning – an approach in which models learn skills through many rounds of trial and error, receiving rewards for getting closer to the desired behavior along with penalties when they diverge from it. But Kazemipour says the unusual geometry of a hand meant they couldn’t just reuse approaches used to train other kinds of legged robots. Standard quadrupeds or bipeds tend to be symmetrical on their left and right sides, which simplifies walking and balance, he says. Hands, in contrast, are not at all symmetrical, with fingers of different lengths and an opposable thumb. In addition to rewards for moving at the right speed and in the right direction and penalties for things like wobbling or jerky movement, the team introduced a novel way to keep the hand in a crawling stance during the simulated training. To account for unequal digit length, they gave each finger its own target position relative to the palm, based on where it naturally sits when in the crawling posture. They then penalized the fingers for straying too far from that reference point, creating what they describe as “virtual springs” that pull the fingers back to the crawling stance. Crucially, the penalties for fingers moving forward and backward are significantly less than those for moving side-to-side, so taking steps in that way costs the hand very little compared with the rewards it receives for moving. The team also trained separate models for skills like righting the hand when it falls over, pressing keys on a keyboard, and pushing objects to a target. All four models fit on the onboard computer, says Kazemipour, and the controller can switch between them as necessary. In real-world tests, the hand crawled across 14 different surfaces including smooth floors, metal grates, grass, and gravel. Other experiments confirmed that it could make both right and left turns, and hit an average speed of 9 centimeters per second. The hand was able to right itself in 21 of 25 trials. When given a video feed from an overhead camera, it even managed to autonomously push a 41-gram cube to targets up to 40 cm away 15 times in a row. “What interests me most about this work is that the same fingers can move the hand, support its weight, and interact with its surroundings,” says Masahiko Inami, a professor at The University of Tokyo whose group has developed hand-shaped walking robots. He agrees that a mobile hand could be useful for reaching confined spaces and operating controls that an entire arm could not easily access, though he says practical deployment would require on-board perception and more robust navigation. Hideki Shimobayashi, a Ph.D. student in Inami’s lab, also points out that walking puts very different loads on a hand compared to grasping, so durability may be a challenge. However, Matei Ciocarlie, an associate professor of mechanical engineering at Columbia University, says it’s a “cool result” that suggests robot hands don’t have to be restricted to the same capabilities as their human counterparts. “One can imagine an entirely new class of mobile manipulators that are simultaneously dexterous, able to traverse complex terrain, and able to manipulate payloads comparable in size to themselves,” he says. Kazemipour sees his work as part of a longer-term vision for robots made up of parts that are not tied to a single job or even a single body plan, something he calls “autonomous modular embodiments.” “Robotic body parts should not be permanently assigned to a single function,” he says. “They can dynamically transition between roles, between being components of one embodiment system and autonomous agents, according to the task.”
